tier_reason: The cited arXiv paper (SPE 2024) numbers match exactly, but they measure the C implementation (lemire/batched_random) against the authors' own unbatched C Fisher-Yates, not std::shuffle. A still holds through Lemire's 2024-08-17 blog post. That post benchmarks std::shuffle against batched_random::shuffle_2 with std::mt19937_64, using public code at lemire/Code-used-on-Daniel-Lemire-s-blog/2024/08/16/benchmarks/stream.cpp (Makefile: -std=c++17 -O3) on an Apple M2 with Apple/LLVM 15. The repo's own benchmarks/benchmark.cpp repeats the same std::shuffle comparison but publishes no numbers.

corrections.claimed_speedup: vs std::shuffle with std::mt19937_64. Apple M2, Apple/LLVM 15 (libc++): 12.4 vs 2.4 ns/element at 10,000 elements and 12.0 vs 2.5 ns/element at 1,000,000 elements (~4.8-5.2x, derived from page data; the author says 'four to five times faster'). Linux, Intel CPU (model not stated), GCC 12 (libstdc++): 2.2 vs 1.7 ns/element at 10,000 and 3.5 vs 2.7 ns/element at 1,000,000 (~1.3x, derived from page data; the author says 'about 30% faster').
corrections.workload: Fisher-Yates shuffle of std::vector<uint64_t> (10,000 and 1,000,000 elements) driven by std::mt19937_64. std::shuffle is compared with batched_random::shuffle_2, which draws two bounded indices from one 64-bit random word using multiplication-based, nearly-divisionless bounded generation.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Apple/LLVM 15 (M2 run); GCC 12 (Linux run); -std=c++17 -O3 per the linked benchmark Makefile
corrections.hardware: Apple M2 MacBook; Linux machine with an Intel processor whose model is not stated
corrections.caveats: The blog numbers were measured with the 2024 prototype header (batched_random::shuffle_2 in lemire/Code-used-on-Daniel-Lemire-s-blog/2024/08/16), the direct predecessor of this repo (created 2025-09). They are not from this repo's current batched_random::shuffle. The gain depends on the standard library: ~4.8-5.2x against libc++ but only ~1.3x against libstdc++, which already uses Lemire's nearly-divisionless bounded method. The peer-reviewed paper (arXiv:2408.06213, SPE 55(1) 2024) reports 1.4-4.7x (Xeon Gold 6338, LLVM 16) and 1.5-3.9x (Apple M2, Apple/LLVM 14). Those paper numbers compare a C implementation against the authors' own unbatched C Fisher-Yates that already uses an efficient bounded-integer method, not against std::shuffle. The header requires a 64-bit URBG and uses static_assert to check it. The repo is dual-licensed MIT and Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception.

notes: The original record credited the paper's 1.4-4.7x to 'std::shuffle-equivalent' and said the page compared against the C++ std directly. Neither holds for the paper, and the libstdc++ gain is only ~1.3x, so the claim was overstated. I moved benchmark_url to the blog post, which compares against std::shuffle directly. The metadata checked out: MIT, 13 stars, last commit 2026-02-28, active.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.5.3 (Intel CPU build); optimization flags not stated in the paper
corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed paper (Salmon, Moraes, Dror & Shaw, 'Parallel Random Numbers: As Easy as 1,2,3', SC11) with a benchmark table (Table 2) that states CPU model and compiler but not flags. The hardware dates from 2011 (Westmere Xeon X5667). On the CPU, only the AES-NI generators (ARS-5 17.8 GB/s, ARS-7 11.1 GB/s) and Threefry-4x64-12 (11.2 GB/s) clearly beat std::mt19937_64 (6.1 GB/s). The recommended portable Threefry-4x64-20 is roughly a tie (6.4 GB/s), and the Philox variants are slower on the CPU (for example Philox4x32-10 at 3.4 GB/s and Philox4x64-10 at 3.9 GB/s). The large wins in the paper are on GPUs, where there is no C++ std baseline. GitHub's license detector reports NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is standard BSD-3-Clause text.

notes: The numbers are accurate, but the evidence is not reproducible to tier A: the flags are missing and the MT timing harness is not public. The last commit on main is 2022-01-17; the record's 2024-02-15 is only the repo's pushed_at timestamp, so the status is abandoned. The paper does not name the standard library, although gcc 4.5.3 implies libstdc++, so I left baseline_stdlib empty.

The benchmark code is public: zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks src/pcg32.cpp and src/std.cpp, with wjakob/pcg32 pinned at 70099ea. The README states clang with -O3 -DNDEBUG and an Intel i5-3570.

corrections.claimed_speedup: pcg32: 940.39M gen/s vs std::mt19937: 270.65M gen/s (~3.47x, derived from page data); pcg32_8 (8-wide header): 944.20M gen/s (~3.49x, derived from page data)
corrections.caveats: Same third-party shootout as the pcg-cpp entry, run on the same 2012-era CPU. The build used no -march flag and the i5-3570 (Ivy Bridge) has no AVX2, so __AVX2__ was undefined. The pcg32_8 row therefore measured the header's scalar fallback path, not the AVX2 path; the table's own remark notes the vectorized version should be faster on capable CPUs. The repo has had no commits since 2016. The license (Apache-2.0) is declared in the source headers, but there is no root LICENSE file, so GitHub's license detector reports none.

notes: The pcg32 ratio 940.393/270.652 is 3.4745, so I corrected ~3.48x to ~3.47x. I also clarified the AVX caveat by checking pcg32_8.h (#if defined(__AVX2__)). The metadata checked out: 88 stars, last commit 2016-06-07, abandoned, Apache-2.0 in headers.
